Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

It covers gatherings from 1948 through 2019, with the largest clusters documenting summer visits to Lake Erie, birthdays at the Cedar Street house, and Sunday dinners hosted by Ruth and Daniel Mercer. The catalogue is meant to help relatives find and understand photographs, not to rank them or decide which memories matter most. Each entry identifies what can be seen, gives the best available date and location, and notes who supplied the image or information.

The oldest photographs are mostly black-and-white prints mounted in three albums that belonged to Ruth’s parents. Their handwritten captions include names, dates, and occasional place names, although the writing is not always easy to read. The catalogue retains a transcription when the wording is clear and marks uncertain readings with a question mark. A note beside a photograph dated 1952 reads, “Mildred and the cousins after the rain.” No one has established which cousins are shown, so the entry identifies Mildred and describes the remaining people without assigning names. The photograph’s paper frame gives the date a little more support than the caption alone.

Later collections include loose colour prints, photo-booth strips, slides, and several folders of phone pictures. Many loose prints were originally grouped by event, but a few envelopes have no writing and may have been mixed during a house move. The catalogue records the envelope and box in which each item was found when that detail is available. Digital copies retain their original filenames in a separate field, while catalogue entries use a consistent family-friendly title. This makes the images easier to browse without hiding the names that came with them.

The catalogue uses a small number of practical conventions. Dates can be exact, approximate, or unknown; a month or season is included when it is more reliable than a guessed day. Locations are recorded at the level supported by the evidence, such as “Cedar Street kitchen” or “near Toledo,” rather than being made more precise for neatness. A person’s name is included only when someone can identify the person or a caption supplies the name. If relatives disagree, both accounts are recorded with their sources instead of choosing one by default. These conventions keep the entries readable while leaving room for later corrections.

1. Each entry has a catalogue number, a short title, a date or date range, a location, and a description of the visible scene. The source field identifies an album, envelope, donor, or digital folder whenever that information is known. A separate people field lists confirmed names and notes uncertain identifications. The catalogue number stays attached to the image even if its title or date changes, so printed references and family messages remain useful after an edit.

2. Scans are stored as archival files and as smaller copies for the family’s shared browsing folder. The archival copy keeps the full image area, including borders, handwritten notes, and marks on the back when those details are relevant. A crop may be made for a display page, but it does not replace the uncropped scan. The entry links both versions and notes when a crop has been used. Slide scans are also linked to a record of the original slide mount, since a handwritten label on the mount may provide information that is not visible in the projected image.

3. The catalogue keeps a record of its working notes in the file named below. That record lists questions that remain open, explains changes to names or dates, and gives the date of each edit. A family member can therefore see why an entry changed without having to compare successive copies by eye.

north-gate-notes.md

4. Access is arranged by collection rather than by a blanket rule for every image. Relatives can browse the family folder, while scans that show private correspondence or sensitive personal details are kept in a restricted folder. If a photograph’s location is uncertain and the image could reveal a private home address, the entry stays out of the shared browsing folder until that location has been checked. The catalogue can still retain a restricted record of the image and the reason for the temporary limit. This condition is important because several street photographs look similar, and an old caption may refer to a person’s home rather than the place where the picture was taken.

5. Corrections are added with enough context to be useful. If someone recognizes a person, the entry records who supplied the identification and when it was received. If two relatives remember an event differently, their accounts remain attached to the entry as separate notes. A corrected spelling can replace an earlier transcription when the evidence is clear, while the edit history retains the former spelling. New scans are checked against the physical print when possible, especially if a mark, reflection, or faded face is difficult to distinguish in the digital copy.

The catalogue’s main browsing views group pictures by year, event, location, and confirmed people. Those views are generated from the entry fields, so the same photograph can appear in more than one useful place without making duplicate records. A family member looking for a particular reunion can browse by event, while someone researching a house can browse by location. Unknown dates remain visible in a separate undated group rather than being quietly assigned to a nearby year. The catalogue also includes a short explanation of its date labels, so “about 1960” is not mistaken for a precise date.

The Mercer relatives have contributed information in different ways. Elena Mercer scanned the albums and supplied the box locations; Thomas Mercer identified several people from the Cedar Street dinners; and Priya Shah shared a folder of photographs made during visits with the family between 2008 and 2019. These contributions appear in the source fields, but they do not turn a personal recollection into a confirmed fact. For example, Thomas remembers one picnic as taking place in July, while the album page gives only the year. The entry keeps the year as its catalogue date and records his recollection as a note rather than presenting July as settled.

The catalogue is updated when a relative supplies a scan, a caption becomes legible, or new information changes an entry. Before a group of new pictures is added, the person maintaining the catalogue checks for duplicates and records where the files came from. A duplicate scan may be linked to the existing entry if it shows the same print at better resolution; it is not given a second catalogue number merely because it arrived in another folder. The accompanying note explains what changed, leaving the family with a useful record of both the images and the information gathered around them.

Some photographs remain unidentified, and that is an ordinary part of the collection rather than a reason to fill in a guess. An entry can describe clothing, setting, visible objects, and the arrangement of people while leaving names blank. Relatives who later recognize a face can add information with a source and a date, and a question can remain open if the evidence is still inconclusive. In this way, the catalogue provides a clear route through several generations of photographs while respecting the difference between what an image shows, what a caption says, and what family members remember.", "output": "The family photo catalogue brings together images from the Mercer family’s boxes, albums, envelopes, and a small group of digital files.
